items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-10-26
items.q: I thought it was all right, but Whiteman never played no jazz. He'd taken all the arrangements from the Dixieland Jazz Band.

ctx.x: And he'd play along with you? Along with me, yes.

And you had two trumpets then? Two trumpets. He played a second. He was a very good harmonist. He was very fast on the catch on the ear. He played piano, but not a jazz piano. I never heard him play on a record, but I did hear him. In 1923 he sat down. And he knew all operatic tunes. He was taught that. He was taught by music. But he became a faker on the carnet. Now that's about all I could tell you outside when he came down here with Whiteman in 1926. I renewed my, or 25, 26, I don't know the exact date…

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1958-06-09
items.q: This were before Paul Whiteman came in the picture... I was asked to record with Whiteman, comma, but could not accept due to a contract with Yerkes, period.

ctx.x: Well, Paul Whiteman, Kid Tua Jazz. Mamie Smith and her jazz hands. I have them records of all of them. Clarence Williams' Blue Five and the Clarence Williams' Blue Rhythm Band, which was featuring Louis Armstrong, Donald Redmond, that's spelled R-E-D-M-O-N-D, Busta Bailey, Coleman Hawkins, etc. Louis Armstrong's first record that brought him recognition was Everybody Loves My Baby, which he recorded with the Clarence Williams' Blue Five. Fletcher Henderson and Benny Morton of Kansas City were also...
They were imitators of the Dixieland Jazz Band. Fletcher Henderson was one of the first colored men to copy from the records of the Dixieland Jazz Band.

items.title: Dominic James "Nick" La Rocca Interview, 1959-06-14
items.q: Even Sharky was imitating Paul Whiteman... I've been told that he's been back here under Dr. Sushant's wing to make a tape recording on jazz. Well, all you had to do is listen to him play with Paul Whiteman and his clarinet.

ctx.x: And they're saying there was some part of the creation of jazz. That Jack Lane, who played a drum and lousy drums at that, created jazz. Now that's good enough for men who thrive on thievery, on a word that we had nothing to do. Our jazz was started in Chicago. We took in the ragtime and changed the rhythm in Chicago. In 1916, we seen we were going to be a flop the first night. And I, being a good dancer, I watched those people. At that time, they had Vernon Castle doing the castle walk. And everybody was trying…

No, I wrote that mostly as a sort of, you might say, editor. Walter Allen managed to interview the various musicians that were still living. And he sent me the facts and I wrote them, sewed them up together. I was more concerned with the records than with the legends. I wasn't very interested in these obscure people from the shadows who were said to have played with this, that and the other musician, in this, that and the other band, and who never made any records at all. I'm not interested in music I can't hear…
